To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the EEG coupling patterns in socially anxious adults undergoing cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for social anxiety disorder normalized by the post treatment assessment; and (b) the clinical group exhibited a greater coupling at pretreat-ment than did post hoc healthy control participants with low levels of social anxiety.

(1) EEG coupling between delta and beta oscillatory activity is enhanced among adults with social anxiety disorder (compared to post hoc controls with low social anxiety) and is reduced by cognitive behavioral therapy; (2) these findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the delta-beta coupling pattern represents a marker for anticipatory anxiety; and (3) EEG delta-beta coupling is a potential neural biomarker that may be useful in identifying adults with SAD who are at risk for poor treatment response.

EEG cross-frequency coupling between the delta and beta bands was elevated at pretreatment among adults with a principal social anxiety disorder diagnosis and that treatment was associated with reductions across multiple symptom measures and informants as well as reductions of EEG cross-frequency coupling.

The main takeaway from our work is that
we found changes in EEG cross-frequency coupling in the delta-beta frequency range during cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for social anxiety disorder (SAD).
the neural changes we observed are associated with the behavioral changes that are associated with psychotherapy, and that these changes occur at multiple levels.
EEG cross-frequency coupling is sensitive to the effects of psychotherapy.
